strategy_title: Autotune XBLOCK Increase Causes Register Spill and Regression
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK configs (256–2048) caused the compiler to allocate significantly more registers per thread (18 → 48), which reduced theoretical occupancy from 100% to 62.5% (limited by register file) and actually lowered achieved occupancy (61.24% → 55.85%). The larger tile sizes also caused a 6.6x increase in executed instructions (12M → 79M) and a 4.8x increase in kernel duration (24.45 µs → 118.24 µs). When a kernel already has low register pressure (≤20 registers/thread) and high theoretical occupancy (100%), adding autotune with large XBLOCK configs can trigger the compiler to unroll more aggressively, inflating register usage and destroying occupancy.
applicable_when: Never applicable as described — this is a negative result. The pattern of adding autotune with large XBLOCK configs is harmful when the kernel already has low register count (≤20 regs/thread) and 100% theoretical occupancy, because the compiler may inflate register usage for larger tile sizes.
do_not_apply_when: Do not add @triton.autotune with large XBLOCK configs (>128) when: (1) registers per thread are already low (≤20), (2) theoretical occupancy is already at or near 100%, (3) the kernel is a simple pointwise op where larger tiles cause the compiler to unroll loops and inflate register pressure. The autotune overhead and register inflation will dominate any tile-size benefit.
framework_notes: In Triton, @triton.autotune with large XBLOCK values causes the JIT compiler to unroll inner loops more aggressively, which can dramatically increase registers per thread even for simple pointwise kernels. The Block Limit Registers dropped from 21 to 5 blocks/SM, capping theoretical occupancy at 62.5%. The grid lambda was also not updated correctly (still used fixed cdiv(N,128) instead of META['XBLOCK']), which may have contributed to the 53.45 waves/SM anomaly.

strategy_title: Doubling num_warps at Fixed XBLOCK Doubles Instructions and Regresses
strategy_description: Increasing num_warps from 4 to 8 (via autotune selecting XBLOCK=128, num_warps=8, which maps to block_size=256) doubled the thread count per block and doubled the total executed instructions (12M → 24M), causing kernel duration to increase from 24.42 µs to 40.67 µs (0.6x speedup). Although achieved occupancy improved (60.67% → 81.23%) and eligible warps per scheduler rose (1.82 → 3.78) as intended, the warp cycles per issued instruction also increased (13.52 → 15.82 cycles), indicating the additional warps did not effectively hide latency but instead added scheduling overhead. The autotune selected block_size=256 (num_warps=8) rather than the intended XBLOCK=128/num_warps=8 configuration, doubling work per block and inflating instruction count — the regression was caused by the autotune config interaction, not the latency-hiding hypothesis itself.
applicable_when: Never applicable as described — this is a negative result. Increasing num_warps via autotune when the kernel is already compute-bound (>60% Compute SOL) and the grid is large (35K+ blocks) does not help because the scheduler already has sufficient wave-level parallelism; adding warps per block only increases per-SM instruction pressure.
do_not_apply_when: Do not increase num_warps via autotune configs for pointwise kernels with: (1) large grid sizes (>10K blocks) providing ample wave-level parallelism, (2) compute SOL already above 60%, (3) warp cycles per issued instruction that are moderate (≤15 cycles) — the additional warps increase total instruction count without proportionally hiding latency, causing regression. Also avoid when the autotune key is coarse (e.g., only 'xnumel') and may select a larger effective block size than intended.
framework_notes: In Triton, num_warps in triton.Config controls threads-per-block as num_warps*32. When XBLOCK=128 but num_warps=8, the block has 256 threads processing 128 elements — each thread does less work but the block still issues the same number of memory transactions. The autotune selected the num_warps=8 config (block_size=256), which doubled total thread count (4.5M → 9M threads) and doubled executed instructions. The float reciprocal rewrite (1.0/tmp6 replacing int32(1)/tmp6) is a valid micro-optimization but was insufficient to overcome the instruction-count regression.

strategy_title: Doubling Block Size to Hide L1TEX Stalls Causes Regression
strategy_description: Doubling block size from 128 to 256 threads (num_warps 4→8) increased achieved occupancy (60.7%→75.2%) and eligible warps per scheduler (1.82→2.31), but the kernel duration increased from 24.42µs to 29.31µs (0.83x speedup). Despite higher occupancy, Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction worsened from 13.52 to 17.23 cycles, and the CPIStall L1TEX stall fraction grew from 43.1% to 55.4% of total cycles, indicating that doubling the block size doubled the pressure on the L1TEX cache and memory pipes (Mem Pipes Busy: 41.6%→59.4%), amplifying rather than hiding the stall. The total executed instructions also increased by ~20% (12.1M→14.5M), and waves per SM doubled (16.7→33.4), adding scheduling overhead without proportional throughput gain.
applicable_when: Never applicable as described — this is a negative result. Increasing num_warps/block_size to hide L1TEX stalls is harmful when the kernel is already compute-bound (SM Throughput ~63%) and the L1TEX stall is caused by memory pressure rather than insufficient in-flight warps.
do_not_apply_when: Do not increase block size (num_warps) to hide L1TEX stalls when: (1) the kernel is already compute-bound (SM SOL >60%), (2) Mem Pipes Busy is already elevated (>40%), (3) the stall is driven by memory bandwidth/pressure rather than pure latency — doubling warps doubles memory pressure and worsens the stall fraction. Also avoid when waves per SM are already high (>16), as doubling waves adds scheduling overhead.
framework_notes: In Triton, increasing num_warps from 4 to 8 with fixed XBLOCK=128 doubles the block size (128→256 threads). The autotune selected num_warps=8 (block_size=256). While register pressure stayed low (18→19 regs/thread) and theoretical occupancy remained 100%, the actual stall cycles per instruction increased because more concurrent warps competed for the same L1TEX bandwidth. The rsqrt replacement (tl.math.rsqrt vs sqrt+int-div) was also applied but could not compensate for the memory pressure regression.
